title: Deepfakes and Misinformation
summary: How fake images, videos, voices and stories are made and spread, how professional fact-checkers catch them, and what you can do to stop them.
learn: The difference between misinformation, disinformation and malinformation
How deepfake images, voices and videos are made
How to use reverse image search, metadata and content credentials
How to check claims using lateral reading and the SIFT method
Why false information spreads so fast online
How the law, platforms and people like you can fight back
intro: Anyone can now make a convincing fake video, voice or news story in minutes. In this topic you learn how deepfakes are made, use the same tools and methods as professional fact-checkers, find out why lies spread faster than the truth, and design a campaign to protect others.

pages.title: Fake news? It's complicated
pages.spec: Explain the difference between misinformation, disinformation and malinformation
pages.summary: Not all false information is the same. Misinformation is false but shared by mistake, disinformation is false and shared on purpose to deceive, and malinformation is true information shared to cause harm.
pages.starter: Your gran shares a post saying "Drinking hot water cures colds!" Is she lying? What's the difference between being wrong and lying?
sc: I can define misinformation, disinformation and malinformation
I can sort real examples into the three types
I can explain why intent matters

b: Misinformation: false, but shared by someone who believes it
Disinformation: false, and shared on purpose to deceive
Malinformation: true, but shared to cause harm
The difference is the intent: what the sharer is trying to do
Money: clicks, adverts and scams
Power: changing how people vote or think
Mischief or revenge: embarrassing someone
Chaos: making people distrust everything
False health information can make people ill
False stories about groups of people can stir up hate
Elections depend on voters having accurate information
If we can't agree on facts, we can't solve problems together

blocks.text: Three types of false or harmful information
People often say "fake news" about anything they disagree with, but experts use more precise words. The key difference is **intent**: whether the person sharing it means to cause harm.

blocks.caption: The three types
head: Type
True or false?
Shared to harm or deceive?
Example
rows: **[[Misinformation]]**
False
No: the sharer believes it
Your gran shares a post claiming hot water cures colds
**[[Disinformation]]**
False
Yes: made to deceive
A fake news website invents a story to get clicks and advert money
**[[Malinformation]]**
True
Yes: shared to hurt
Someone posts a classmate's real but private messages to embarrass them

blocks.text: Disinformation often **becomes** misinformation: someone makes a fake on purpose, then thousands of people share it believing it's real.
Why does anyone make it?

blocks.title: Common motives for disinformation
items: Money: shocking stories get clicks, and clicks earn advertising money
Influence: trying to change how people think or vote
Scams: tricking people into handing over money or details
Harm: bullying, revenge or stirring up hatred against a group

blocks.text: Satire (like a joke news website) isn't meant to deceive, but it can turn into misinformation when people share it without realising it's a joke.

blocks.title: Sort the stories
steps: Read the eight short scenarios on the board or card set.
Decide whether each is misinformation, disinformation, malinformation, or true and harmless.
For each one, write the clue that helped you decide.

q.q: Which scenario was hardest to sort, and why?
q.a: Answers vary. A common one is satire shared as fact: the original creator wasn't trying to deceive, but the person sharing it spread misinformation.

q.q: Explain why the person's intent matters when we decide how to respond.
q.a: If someone shared misinformation by mistake, we can gently correct them; disinformation and malinformation are deliberate and may need reporting, as they can be bullying, scams or even crimes.

check.q: What is misinformation?
o: False information shared by someone who believes it

check.q: What is disinformation?
o: False information created or shared on purpose to deceive

check.q: Someone posts a classmate's real private messages to humiliate them. This is...
Why do some websites make up shocking stories?

practice.a: Misinformation: false, shared without intending harm/believed true (1); disinformation: false, shared deliberately to deceive (1); malinformation: true but shared to cause harm (1).

practice.q: Give two reasons why someone might create disinformation.
practice.a: Any two: money/clicks/adverts (1); influence voters/opinions (1); scams (1); revenge/bullying (1); cause chaos/distrust (1).

pages.title: How deepfakes are made
pages.spec: Describe how AI is used to create deepfake images, voices and videos
pages.summary: Deepfakes are realistic fake media made with AI: face swaps, lip-syncing, voice clones and fully generated video. They are made by training AI on examples of a person and are getting easier and cheaper to create.
pages.starter: How many photos of your face do you think are online right now? Who could use them?
sc: I can describe four types of deepfake
I can explain how AI learns to copy a face or voice
I can explain why deepfakes are getting harder to spot

b: Fake image, audio or video made with AI that looks or sounds like a real person
The name comes from "deep learning" + "fake"
Can show someone doing or saying something they never did
Tools are now free, fast and run on a phone
Face swap: one person's face placed onto another's body
Lip-sync: real video, but the mouth is changed to match new words
Voice clone: a copy of someone's voice from a few seconds of audio
Fully generated: a whole video or photo created from a text prompt
It studies many examples of a face or voice
It learns patterns: how the face moves, how the voice sounds
It then generates new frames or sounds that fit those patterns
More examples = more convincing fake
slides.n: Point out that celebrities and politicians are easy targets because there are thousands of hours of their video online. This is also why pupils should think about what they post.

blocks.text: What is a deepfake?

A **[[deepfake]]** is an image, audio clip or video made or changed by AI so that it looks or sounds like a real person doing or saying something they never did. The name combines **deep learning** (a type of AI) with **fake**. Deepfakes are a kind of **[[generative AI]]** output.
Types of deepfake

blocks.caption: Common kinds of deepfake
head: Type
How it works
Example
rows: **[[face swap|Face swap]]**
Puts one person's face onto someone else's body in a video
A film clip with a different actor's face
Lip-sync
Changes the mouth in a real video so it matches new words
A politician "saying" something they never said
**[[voice clone|Voice clone]]**
Copies a voice from a few seconds of recordings
A scam phone call in a family member's voice
Fully generated
Creates the whole image or video from a text prompt
A photo of an event that never happened

blocks.text: How the AI learns

To fake a particular person, an AI model is trained on examples: photos, videos or recordings of them. It learns patterns such as the shape of their face from every angle and the rhythm of their voice. Then it can generate new pictures or sounds that fit those patterns. The more examples it has, the more convincing the fake. That's why public figures (with hours of video online) are common targets, and why you should think about what you share.
Making a deepfake of a real person without their consent is wrong, even as a joke. Fake sexual images of real people are illegal, and making or sharing them can lead to criminal charges.
Getting harder to spot

Early deepfakes had obvious glitches: blurry edges, strange blinking, mouths that didn't match the sound. Newer tools fix many of these problems, and they keep improving. So spotting deepfakes by eye alone is no longer reliable: you need to check the **source** as well as the content (lesson 3 and 4).

blocks.title: Deepfake detectives
steps: Your teacher shows six short clips or images (some real, some AI-made, all of fictional or consenting people).
For each one, decide real or fake and write the clue you used.
Your teacher reveals the answers: how many did you get right?

q.q: How many did you get right, and which clue was most useful?
q.a: Answers vary. Most people score worse than they expect, which shows why visual clues alone aren't enough.

q.q: Why might checking the source be more reliable than looking for glitches?
q.a: AI tools keep improving so glitches disappear, but a fake usually can't come from a trusted original source, so checking where it came from still works.

check.q: What is a deepfake?
o: AI-made media showing a real person doing or saying something they didn't
check.why: Deepfakes fake real people with AI.

check.q: What does a voice clone do?
check.why: Voice cloning imitates a real voice.

check.q: Why are celebrities easy targets for deepfakes?
o: There is lots of video and audio of them online to train AI

check.q: Why is spotting deepfakes by eye becoming less reliable?
o: AI tools keep improving and remove obvious glitches
check.why: Better tools mean fewer visible errors.

practice.q: Describe how an AI system is able to create a voice clone of a person.
practice.a: It is trained on recordings/examples of the person's voice (1) and learns the patterns of how they sound, then generates new speech that fits those patterns (1).

practice.q: Give one harmful and one helpful use of voice-cloning technology, and explain why consent matters.
practice.a: Harmful: e.g. scam calls, fake recordings (1); helpful: e.g. people who've lost their voice, dubbing films with permission (1); consent: the person's voice/identity belongs to them and they should control how it's used (1).

pages.title: Fact-checker's toolkit
pages.spec: Use reverse image search, metadata and content credentials to investigate images
pages.summary: Professional fact-checkers use tools as well as their eyes. Reverse image search finds where a picture first appeared, metadata can reveal when and how a file was made, and content credentials show a file's history.
pages.starter: A photo shows a shark swimming down a flooded motorway. How could you find out if it's real?
sc: I can use a reverse image search to find a picture's origin
I can explain what metadata is and what it can show
I can explain what content credentials are

b: Reverse image search: search with a picture instead of words
Shows where else the image appears online, and often the original
Old photos are often reshared as if they were new
Try Google Lens, Bing Visual Search or TinEye
slides.n: The "shark on a motorway" is a famous fake that reappears after almost every big flood.

b: Metadata is hidden information stored with a file
Photos can hold the date, the camera or phone, settings and sometimes location
Missing or odd metadata can be a clue, but isn't proof
Social media usually strips metadata when you upload
Provenance means the history of where something came from
Content credentials are a new standard (C2PA) that records how a file was made and edited
Some cameras and AI tools add them automatically
Look for the "CR" icon or check with a content credentials inspector

blocks.text: Search with a picture

A **[[reverse image search]]** lets you search using an image instead of words. It finds other places the picture appears online and similar pictures. This is one of the most powerful checks you can do, because many viral "news" photos are actually old pictures from different events, or have been edited from an original you can find.

blocks.title: The flooded-motorway shark
blocks.context: After a hurricane, a photo of a shark swimming on a flooded motorway goes viral.
steps: Do a reverse image search with the photo.
Results show the same shark picture shared after many different storms over several years.
Earlier results lead to the original: a shark photo from a magazine and a separate photo of a flooded road, combined in editing software.
blocks.answer: The image is fake: an edited composite reshared after each new flood. A reverse image search exposed it in under a minute.

blocks.text: Metadata

**[[metadata]]** is "data about data": hidden information saved with a file. A photo's metadata (called EXIF data) can include the date and time it was taken, the phone or camera model, and sometimes GPS location. Fact-checkers look for clues: a "new" photo with a date from five years ago, or editing software listed where a camera should be.
Metadata can also reveal your location. Many apps remove it when you post, but not all do. Check your phone's camera settings.
Content credentials and provenance

**[[provenance]]** means the history of where something came from. **[[content credentials]]** are a new industry standard (from a group called C2PA, which includes camera makers, news organisations and tech companies) that attaches a secure record to a file showing who made it, with what tool, and how it was edited, including whether AI was used. Some phone cameras and AI image generators add them automatically, so a "Made with AI" label can travel with the picture.
No single tool proves an image is real. Fact-checkers combine clues: the source, reverse search results, metadata, credentials and common sense.

blocks.title: Investigate the viral image
steps: Your teacher gives you three images that "went viral".
For each, do a reverse image search and note the earliest date and original source you can find.
Look for any metadata or content credentials (your teacher may provide the files).
Write a verdict: real, real but old/misleading, edited, or AI-generated, and your evidence.

q.q: Write your verdict and evidence for one image.
q.a: Example: "Real but misleading: reverse search shows it was taken in 2017 in another country, not at last week's storm here. Earliest copy: a news agency website."

q.q: Which tool was most useful, and why?
q.a: Usually reverse image search, because it shows where and when the image first appeared; metadata is often stripped by social media.

check.q: What does a reverse image search do?
o: Searches the web using a picture to find where it appears
check.why: You search with an image instead of words.

check.q: What is metadata?
o: Hidden information stored with a file, such as date and device

check.q: What are content credentials?
o: A secure record of how a file was made and edited
check.why: They record a file's history, including AI use.

check.q: A "new" storm photo appears in search results from years ago. What does this suggest?
o: It's an old photo being reshared as new
check.why: Recycled photos are a common trick.

practice.q: Explain how a reverse image search can help show that a photo is misleading.
practice.a: It finds earlier copies/the original source of the image (1), which can show it's from a different time/place or has been edited (1).

practice.q: Give two pieces of information that photo metadata might contain.
practice.a: Any two: date/time taken (1); camera/phone model (1); location/GPS (1); camera settings (1); editing software (1).

pages.title: Think like a fact-checker
pages.spec: Check claims using lateral reading and the SIFT method
pages.summary: Professional fact-checkers don't just study a website: they leave it and see what other trusted sources say about it. The SIFT method (Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace to the original) is a quick routine anyone can use.
pages.starter: A website looks really professional and says it's "independent". Does that mean you can trust it?
sc: I can use the four steps of SIFT
I can read laterally to check a source
I can judge whether a source is reliable

b: Looking professional doesn't make a site reliable
Fact-checkers read laterally: they open new tabs to see what others say about the source
Students who read "vertically" (staying on the page) are much easier to fool
Lateral reading is quicker and more accurate
Stop: notice your emotions and don't share yet
Investigate the source: who made this and why?
Find better coverage: do trusted outlets report it?
Trace claims, quotes and media back to the original
Who is behind it, and do they have expertise?
Does it have a reason to mislead (money, politics)?
Do other reliable sources say the same?
Is it up to date, and does it link to evidence?

blocks.text: Lateral reading

When you check a website, the natural thing is to read it carefully from top to bottom. Professional fact-checkers do something different: **[[lateral reading]]**. They leave the page almost straight away and open new tabs to find out what **other** trusted sources say about the website or claim. Research has found this is faster and much more accurate than studying the page itself, because a misleading site can look very professional.
The SIFT method
**[[SIFT]]** is a four-step routine created by digital literacy expert Mike Caulfield.

items: **Stop.** If a post makes you feel shocked, angry or excited, pause. Strong emotions are exactly what disinformation is designed to cause.
**Investigate the source.** Who made this? Search for the person or organisation. Are they experts? Do they have a reason to mislead?
**Find better coverage.** Search for the claim itself. Are trusted news organisations or fact-checkers (like BBC Verify or Full Fact) reporting it?
**Trace claims, quotes and media to the original.** Find where the quote, statistic or picture really came from. Was it taken out of context?

blocks.title: SIFTing a claim
blocks.context: A post says: "Scientists confirm mobile phones will be banned in all schools next month!" It links to a site called "UK Education Truth".
steps: Stop: it's surprising and makes people angry or excited, so pause.
Investigate: searching "UK Education Truth" shows it's an anonymous site with no named writers, known for clickbait.
Find better coverage: the BBC and gov.uk have no such announcement.
Trace: the "scientists" quote comes from an unrelated report about screen time, with the ban added by the site.
blocks.answer: Disinformation. Four quick checks, about three minutes.

blocks.text: Judging a source

A **[[source]]** is where information comes from. Reliable sources are usually open about who they are, have relevant expertise, correct their mistakes, back up claims with evidence and are reported on positively by other trusted sources.

blocks.title: SIFT race
steps: Your teacher gives each pair four claims found online.
Use the SIFT steps to check each claim. Time yourselves.
Record what you found at each step and your verdict.

q.q: Choose one claim. Write what you found for each SIFT step.
q.a: A good answer records a pause/emotional reaction, what was found about the source, whether trusted outlets reported it, and where the claim/picture originally came from, ending with a clear verdict.
Disinformation is designed to trigger strong emotions so we share quickly without thinking; pausing gives us time to check.

check.q: What is lateral reading?
o: Reading a page from top to bottom
Leaving a page to check what other sources say about it

check.q: What does the S in SIFT stand for first?
check.why: Stop before you react or share.

check.q: What does "Trace claims to the original" mean?
o: Find where a quote, statistic or picture really came from

check.q: Which is a sign a source may be unreliable?
o: No named authors and a history of clickbait

practice.q: Describe the four steps of the SIFT method.
practice.a: Stop: pause/notice emotion before sharing (1); Investigate the source: who made it and why (1); Find better coverage: check trusted outlets (1); Trace claims/media to the original context (1).

practice.q: Explain why lateral reading is more effective than studying a website closely.
practice.a: Misleading sites can look professional/convincing (1); checking what other trusted sources say about the site/claim reveals its reliability more quickly/accurately (1).

pages.title: Why lies travel fast
pages.spec: Explain why false information spreads quickly online
pages.summary: False stories often spread faster than true ones because they are surprising and emotional. Recommendation algorithms reward engagement, bots and fake accounts amplify messages, and echo chambers mean we see what we already believe.
pages.starter: Which post would you be more likely to share: "Local council meeting goes well" or "SHOCKING: what they're hiding at the council"? Why?
sc: I can explain how emotion makes content spread
I can explain how algorithms and bots amplify content
I can describe echo chambers and filter bubbles

b: Content that causes shock, anger or fear gets shared most
False stories are often more surprising than true ones
A famous study found false news reached people much faster than true news on Twitter
Sharing takes one tap; checking takes effort
slides.n: The study is Vosoughi, Roy and Aral, Science 2018, which found falsehood diffused "farther, faster, deeper and more broadly" than truth.

b: Platform algorithms choose what you see, often by engagement: likes, comments, shares, watch time
Outrage gets engagement, so it can get promoted
Bots: automated accounts that post and share at huge scale
Coordinated fake accounts can make a few people look like a crowd
Filter bubble: the algorithm shows you more of what you already like
Echo chamber: you mostly hear from people who agree with you
Inside a bubble, false claims go unchallenged
Following a wide range of trusted sources helps you see more of the picture

blocks.text: Why do false stories spread?

Researchers have found that false stories often spread further and faster online than true ones. One reason is **novelty**: made-up stories are often more surprising. Another is **emotion**: posts that make us shocked, angry or afraid are shared more, often before anyone checks them.
Algorithms and engagement

On social media, an **[[algorithm]]** decides which posts appear in your feed. Many feeds are designed to keep you on the app, so they prioritise **[[engagement]]**: likes, comments, shares and watch time. Outrageous or emotional posts get lots of engagement (even angry comments count), so the algorithm may show them to even more people.
Bots and fake accounts

A **[[bot]]** is an automated account run by software. Networks of bots and fake accounts can post thousands of times an hour, make a hashtag trend, or make a false claim look popular. When something seems popular, real people are more likely to believe and share it.
Filter bubbles and echo chambers

blocks.caption: Bubbles and chambers
head: Term
What it means
Effect
rows: **[[filter bubble|Filter bubble]]**
The algorithm shows you more of what you already click on
You see less that challenges your view
**[[echo chamber|Echo chamber]]**
You mostly follow and talk with people who agree with you
False claims that fit the group's views go unquestioned

blocks.text: To burst your bubble: follow a range of reliable sources, search for the other side of a story, and be suspicious of posts that make you very angry.

blocks.title: Trace the spread
steps: Your teacher shows how a made-up story about a local school spread over 24 hours (a simulation with fictional accounts).
Mark on the timeline where the story got a boost: an emotional headline, a bot network, an influencer share, the algorithm.
Mark the three points where someone could have stopped it.

q.q: Name two things that helped the story spread and explain how.
q.a: E.g. an emotional headline made people share without checking; bots shared it hundreds of times so it trended; the algorithm showed it to more people because it got lots of comments.

q.q: Where could the spread have been stopped, and by whom?
q.a: E.g. the first sharers could have checked (SIFT); the platform could have labelled or slowed it; a fact-checker or the school could have posted a correction early.

check.q: Why do emotional posts spread quickly?
o: People share them before thinking or checking

check.q: What is engagement on social media?
o: Likes, comments, shares and watch time
The number of followers you block

check.q: What is a bot?
o: An automated account run by software

check.q: What is a filter bubble?
o: When the algorithm keeps showing you what you already like

practice.q: Explain how a social media algorithm can help false information spread.
practice.a: Algorithms often promote content with high engagement (1); false/emotional/outrageous posts get lots of likes/comments/shares (1); so the algorithm shows them to more people, spreading them further (1).

practice.q: Describe the difference between a filter bubble and an echo chamber.
practice.a: Filter bubble: the algorithm shows you more of what you already like/click (1); echo chamber: you mainly hear from people who share your views (1).

pages.title: Fighting back
pages.spec: Describe how the law, platforms and individuals can reduce the harm of deepfakes and misinformation
pages.summary: Laws, platform rules, fact-checkers and new technology all help, but individuals matter too. "Prebunking" (warning people about tricks before they meet them) works, and everyone can check, correct kindly and report.
pages.starter: If you saw a friend share something false, would you tell them? How would you do it without starting an argument?
sc: I can describe how laws and platforms tackle harmful fakes
I can explain what prebunking is
I can design a campaign to protect others

b: The UK's Online Safety Act makes big platforms deal with illegal and harmful content
Sharing intimate images of someone without consent, including deepfakes, is a crime in the UK
Platforms have rules: removing, labelling or slowing false and harmful posts
Elections have rules about who pays for political adverts
slides.n: Keep the legal detail general. Emphasise: never create or share fake images of real people, and report it if it happens to you.

b: Professional fact-checkers: Full Fact, BBC Verify, FactCheckNI
Content credentials and AI labels (lesson 3)
Community notes: users add context to misleading posts
Teachers, parents and trusted adults
Prebunking: learning the tricks before you meet them, like a vaccine
Spot the tricks: fake experts, emotional language, out-of-context pictures, impersonation
Correct kindly and privately, with a good source
Report harmful fakes; never pass them on

blocks.text: The law and the platforms

In the UK, the **[[Online Safety Act]]** requires social media and search companies to protect users from illegal content and to protect children from harmful content. Sharing intimate images of someone without their consent is a crime, and that includes AI-made deepfakes. Platforms also have their own rules and may remove posts, add warning labels or show them to fewer people.

If someone makes or shares a fake image of you or someone you know: don't share it, screenshot it as evidence, report it on the platform, and tell a trusted adult. In serious cases the police can help.
Fact-checkers and new tech

A **[[fact-checker]]** is a person or organisation that investigates claims and publishes what's true. Examples include Full Fact, BBC Verify and FactCheckNI in Northern Ireland. Technology helps too: content credentials, AI-detection tools and "community notes", where users add context to misleading posts.
Prebunking

Researchers have found that one of the best defences is **[[prebunking]]**: learning about manipulation tricks **before** you encounter them. It works like a vaccine: a weak dose of the trick helps you recognise the real thing later.

blocks.title: Common manipulation tricks
items: Fake experts: someone with impressive-sounding titles but no real expertise
Emotional language: ALL CAPS, "SHOCKING", "they don't want you to know"
Out of context: real photos or quotes from a different time or place
Impersonation: fake accounts pretending to be a real person or organisation
False choices: "Either you agree with this or you hate our town"

blocks.text: Correcting kindly

If a friend or relative shares something false, telling them publicly can make them defensive. It's usually better to message them privately, be kind, share a reliable source and explain how you checked.

blocks.title: Prebunk campaign
steps: Choose one manipulation trick from the list.
Design a short prebunking campaign for Year 7: a poster, a 30-second video script or a set of three social media posts.
Show the trick with a made-up, harmless example (no real people), and give one tip for spotting it.
Present to another group and give each other feedback.

q.q: Which trick did you choose, and what is your one-sentence tip for spotting it?
q.a: E.g. "Out of context: before you share a dramatic photo, do a reverse image search to see where and when it was really taken."

q.q: Write a kind private message you could send to a friend who shared a false post.
q.a: E.g. "Hey, I saw that post about the school closing. I checked the school website and the BBC and they say it's not true. The photo is from 2019. Thought you'd want to know!"

check.q: What does the Online Safety Act require big platforms to do?
o: Protect users from illegal content and children from harmful content
check.why: It sets safety duties for platforms.

check.q: What is prebunking?
o: Correcting a post after it spreads
Learning about manipulation tricks before you meet them

check.q: What is the best way to correct a friend who shared something false?
o: Ignore it and share it too
Message them privately and kindly with a reliable source

check.q: Which organisation fact-checks claims in Northern Ireland?

practice.q: Describe three things a pupil should do if a fake image of them is shared online.
practice.a: Any three: don't share it further (1); screenshot/save evidence (1); report it to the platform (1); tell a trusted adult/teacher (1); contact police in serious cases (1).

practice.q: Explain why prebunking can be effective.
practice.a: Learning the tricks in advance helps people recognise them (1) when they meet real disinformation, so they're less likely to believe/share it, like a vaccine (1).

Checking a source by leaving it and seeing what other trusted sources say about it.

Where a piece of information comes from.
A set of rules a computer follows; on social media, the rules that choose what appears in your feed.
How people interact with content: likes, comments, shares and watch time.
An automated account run by software rather than a person.
A space where you mostly hear from people who already agree with you.
When an algorithm keeps showing you content similar to what you already like, so you see fewer other views.
Learning about manipulation tricks before you encounter them, so you can recognise them.
A person or organisation that investigates claims and publishes what is true.
